item.title: Former Bernie Sanders operative warns radical left has 'overtaken' the Democratic Party from within
item.description: A former Bernie Sanders operative warned the Democratic Party has been overtaken by its far-left flank through radicalized donors and staffers.
item.content:encoded:
A former Bernie Sanders operative is sounding the alarm over what the Democratic Party has become, warning that the far left has "overtaken" the party from within.

"Part of the reason it's been overtaken is because the establishment tried really hard in 2020 to block us, and in 2019, after AOC won, they did a blacklist and that actually backfired on them, and it made the far left grow stronger," Evan Barker told "Jesse Watters Primetime."

Barker, who raised money for Democratic candidates throughout her career before deciding to vote for Trump in 2024, argued that the Democratic establishment's efforts to contain its insurgent flank ultimately backfired, pushing activists to build their own political infrastructure — from training one another to recruiting donors, including billionaires.

EX-DEM OPERATIVE DETAILS 'NEW DONOR ESTABLISHMENT' BEHIND MAMDANI-ERA PROGRESSIVES: 'NOT FROM THE GRASSROOTS'

The result, Barker argued, is a party increasingly influenced from the inside by its activist base, donors and staffers, some of whom she says are considerably further left than the politicians they work for.

"I think they've kind of been captured from all sides. They have these hyper-left-leaning donors coupled with the staff that's been radicalized and the base," she said.

Barker said she has watched that shift play out even within the movement she once joined, pointing to Sanders' positions on issues including guns and immigration.

"I've seen him kind of be dragged further and further to the left by what he views as his message bearers, people like AOC and Ilhan Omar and now Abdul El-Sayed," she added.

DEMS' LEFTWARD LURCH GETS LEGS AS EL-SAYED'S MICHIGAN SENATE VICTORY SPARKS PARTY DEBATE

Barker's warning comes as a new crop of progressive candidates and democratic socialists test its strength ahead of the midterm elections, including figures she says are carrying forward the movement that Sanders helped build.

Progressive Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, whom Barker specifically named as one of Sanders' emerging "message bearers," recently secured the Democratic nomination in a close primary against Rep. Haley Stevens.

Others have won key primaries elsewhere, including Mamdani-backed Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York.

Barker previously revealed to Fox News Digital that the Democratic Party's leftward shift prompted her decision to leave the party, sharing that she was inspired to enter politics during former President Barack Obama's 2008 campaign.

"If you look at him then, and you compare him to the modern movement of the party today, it is just night and day. They have gone left on so many critical issues, like immigration and identity politics, and defund the police and just all of these things that I did not sign up for," she said.

She added that former President Joe Biden's withdrawal from the 2024 presidential race and then-Vice President Kamala Harris' subsequent nomination made her recognize in "real time the manifestation of everything the Democrats had become."

Fox News' Robert McGreevy contributed to this report.

item.title: Seaweed-based coating could keep strawberries fresh for days without refrigeration, study finds
item.description: UBC researchers developed a seaweed-based coating that kept strawberries fresh for four days without refrigeration, doubling shelf life of produce.
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve ever brought home a carton of fresh strawberries only to find them moldy and destined for the trash a few days later, researchers may have found a simple solution: coating the fruit in a seaweed-based liquid that could keep it fresh without refrigeration.

University of British Columbia (UBC) scientists developed the seaweed-derived coating with the goal of extending the shelf life of fresh produce and reducing food waste and reliance on energy-intensive refrigeration.

"Nearly half of all food produced in Canada is lost or wasted, costing the economy an estimated $58 billion annually," the university reported in a news release on the seaweed-coating breakthrough. "Fresh fruits and vegetables are particularly vulnerable to spoilage, losing moisture and becoming susceptible to mold and bacteria during storage and transport."

EATING 5 FRUITS AND VEGETABLES A DAY MAY NOT BE ENOUGH FOR HEART HEALTH, STUDY FINDS

According to UBC, researchers developed the "natural, biocompatible, plant-based, and consumer-friendly" coating for post-harvest preservation by combining agar, a substance derived from red seaweed; with zinc, an essential nutrient; and tannic acid, a naturally occurring plant compound found in foods and beverages such as grapes and tea.

"Applied to strawberries, grapes and apple slices, the coating extended shelf life by at least two-fold," the researchers reported in their study, published in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry.

"The coating acts like a very thin and invisible protective barrier," Tianxi Yang, a UBC assistant professor of food science and the study's lead author, told Fox News Digital. "It helps slow moisture loss and gas exchange while also providing antibacterial and antioxidant protection, which together delay dehydration, softening, oxidation and spoilage."

The shelf life of an average carton of strawberries could be extended considerably with this coating, Yang said.

"At room temperature, uncoated strawberries showed visible spoilage within about two days, while coated strawberries remained fresh and intact for at least four days," she said. "When the coating was combined with refrigeration, we observed no spoilage for at least six days."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

The coating is designed to be essentially tasteless and preserve the produce’s natural flavor, Yang said. Initial observations suggest the coating does not noticeably change the strawberries’ smell, texture or natural appearance.

Yang added that she and fellow researchers plan to conduct comprehensive sensory studies soon.

According to the UBC release, "the coating also showed antibacterial properties and no signs of toxicity in tests using human intestinal cells." The coating has not yet been approved for commercial use.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For consumers concerned about ingesting the coating, researchers found that most of it can be easily rinsed off under running tap water.

Further safety assessments and regulatory review would still be required before commercial use, Yang noted, but she said the results so far are encouraging.

"The technology has demonstrated promising performance and scalability in the laboratory," she said.

"The next steps will focus on further safety and regulatory evaluation, scale-up and commercial validation. We are also interested in connecting with potential investors and partners who can help advance the technology toward commercialization."

item.title: Ted Cruz, conservatives respond after Talarico criticizes Bible-related education in schools as 'propaganda'
item.description: A resurfaced video showed Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico calling Texas' Bluebonnet curriculum "propaganda," drawing Sen. Ted Cruz's rebuke.
item.content:encoded:
Texas state representative and Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico’s campaign responded after a resurfaced video of his comments on the Bible and education sparked outrage.

A clip resurfaced this week of Talarico, a Christian seminarian, speaking in a video hosted by the Center for American Progress Action Fund in 2025. In the clip, the host asked Talarico about his legislative battles with "Christian Nationalists," meaning people who consider America to be an inherently Christian nation. 

The portion that went viral recently when Talarico blasted the "most insidious" legislation he fought to stop while serving in Texas government, claiming one bill required schools in the state to teach Bible stories as historical fact. He argued that this amounted to pushing "propaganda" on children and was not just bad for state schools, but for society overall.

"It was a new state curriculum that would teach Christian Bible stories as historical fact, as the only truth to our youngest students, and I mean kindergarten, first graders," he said. "These are kids who aren’t able to think for themselves yet. They haven’t formed their own worldviews."

TEXAS DEM NOMINEE JAMES TALARICO INVOKES FAITH TO DEFEND ABORTION RIGHTS, ‘THE BIBLE IS SILENT ON ABORTION'

He further warned that the alleged effort to "push propaganda, to push indoctrination on those youngest students is deeply immoral and should trouble all of us."

Sen. Ted Cruz. R-Texas, retweeted the clip, asking a brief, "Um, wut?" alongside numerous other commentators.

"The claim made by Representative Talarico is misleading," Mary Elizabeth Castle, director of government relations for Texas Values told Fox News Digital. "The curriculum he was referring to in the video from 2025 is the Bluebonnet curriculum, which was an English Language Arts curriculum adopted in the winter of 2024 that helped students understand the copious amounts of Bible references made in historical speeches and common stories like Dr. Martin Luther King’s ‘I Have a Dream’ speech." 

"The references to the Bible in the Bluebonnet curriculum help students understand the thousands of everyday idioms that people use every day that have some context to Scripture," she continued. 

"The Bluebonnet curriculum was defended by top religious liberty law firms like First Liberty Institute and high elected officials like Dr. Ben Carson," Castle added. "The purpose of the biblical references was to improve reading scores and reading comprehension among students. The majority of Texas parents and stakeholders testified in favor of the curriculum, which passed at the State Board of Education. A very small number of people would agree with Mr. Talarico’s sentiment and a number of school districts have purchased this curriculum."

POWERFUL LGBTQ+ GROUP'S ENDORSEMENTS COULD TANK VULNERABLE DEMS OVER RADICAL YOUTH TRANS AGENDA

First Liberty executive general counsel Hiram Sasser told Fox News Digital, "Courts across the nation have determined that the Bible has had profound influence on Western culture and is an important piece of literature and history. No education is complete without understanding the Bible and its influence, as even the ACLU recognizes. What is crazy is that Talarico is to the Left of the ACLU, which agreed in a court settlement with us that the Bible may be taught in Texas schools."

"Democrats have a funny way of defining ‘indoctrination.’ When they do it, it's ‘inclusion.’ When it opposes their ideology, it's considered government-imposed cruelty," Tim Graham, the executive editor of Media Research Center's NewsBusters, told Fox News Digital. "Talarico has clearly and repeatedly identified himself as a pusher of leftist gender ideology, which stands in dramatic contradiction to biblical teaching. So it's not shocking he doesn't want anybody discussing the Bible in the classroom."

A spokesperson for Talarico's campaign told Fox News Digital, "James is a Christian seminarian who’s dedicated his life to the teachings of Jesus Christ — fighting religious and political corruption when he sees it because there’s nothing Christ-like about powerful people using scripture to score political points. While billionaire-bought politicians like Ken Paxton attack James for his faith — he will continue encouraging Texans across the political spectrum to come together by loving their neighbors as themselves."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

In an interview with podcaster Joe Rogan, Talarico shared his personal views on the importance of the separation of church and state, even as a Christian seminarian.

"As a Christian, I think my concern is for the Muslim kid and the Jewish kid, the Hindu kid, the atheist kid who’s sitting in a classroom who now has a poster on the wall forced by the government that says, you know, your religion is inferior, or you're not welcome here," he had said. "And I just think if Jesus saw that, he would weep for those students and would demand that we love them as ourselves. And so that's why I kind of spoke out against the bill on theological grounds, not just constitutional grounds."

Talarico’s campaign has also drawn criticism over his support for raising children as transgender, though he has drawn a line regarding procedures such as gender reassignment surgeries for minors, a policy he explicitly opposed in a June interview.

item.title: Sophie Cunningham supporters rally in Indiana while displaying what makes America great
item.description: Sophie Cunningham supporters rallied outside the Indiana Fever game, uniting Democrats and conservatives to keep women's sports female.
item.content:encoded:
A large group of female activists, moms, and concerned citizens rallied again this week outside an Indiana Fever game in support of Sophie Cunningham and keeping women’s sports female. On Friday evening just outside of the Gainbridge Fieldhouse, they made their voices heard.

After traveling to Portland and Chicago, I witnessed firsthand how refreshingly normal Indiana Fever games felt both outside the arena and inside. The crowds were vocally supportive of the women, and the few men accompanying them. Many Fever fans gave the Cunningham rally crowd a thumbs up, some provided encouraging words, and others stopped to take photos with the almost life-size Sophie Cunningham poster.

It was a nice change of pace compared to the radical, profane, aggressive trans protesters they have had to face in other cities.

Shockingly to much of the WNBA and liberal media, this group isn’t just a bunch of conservatives, who completely align on all of their politics. It’s a diverse group of people that represent a beautiful mix of registered Democrats, conservatives and people from a wide range of backgrounds and communities.

It’s not some sort of MAGA coalition, which many love to claim. It’s a group that represents what America should, and used to like: Almost three dozen citizens agree that women’s sports and spaces should remain female, though disagreeing on a litany of other issues, while supporting the one female professional athlete courageously willing to stand up for what’s right.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SEES SUPPORT SURGE AFTER STAR PUTS CAREER ON LINE FOR GIRLS SPORTS

Kara Dansky, a registered Democrat who serves on the board for Democrats for an Informed Approach to Gender, told me, "The truth of the matter is, the clear majority of registered Democrats in this country are aligned on these topics."

She went on to diagnose the problem from the top down in Washington, D.C., and across the country, saying, "The problem is that our elected officials are selling out women and girls. They’re selling out children at the altar of a cult."

When asking Dansky what she’d say to WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert, who put together a task force of general managers and team presidents to tackle the transgender issue the league faces, she didn’t hold back.

"There are girls watching today. There are girls that do not understand what Title IX meant in 1972 to women like you, who have benefited from Title IX. You owe these girls commitment to female only sports."

HHS OFFICIAL WARNS OF IRREVERSIBLE RISKS AS TRUMP ADMIN RESTRICTS FUNDING FOR YOUTH GENDER PROCEDURES

A group called LGB Courage Coalition also rallied outside the Fever vs. Wings game with a gigantic sign that said: "Chemical castration isn’t medicine. Save girls’ sports. Save boys’ bodies."

LGB Courage Coalition Executive Director Jamie Reid, who is a whistleblower from a pediatric gender center said, "I participated in medically transitioning kids… I [now] work to try to stop transitions and I think that it is incredibly tied up with the sports movement right now."

When asking Reid what she would tell the WNBA Commissioner and her task force from her unique perspective, she said: "At the bottom line, this is about medical evidence. There is no good medical evidence to support the medical transition of any minor. We know at that basis, we don’t have to be so wrapped up in the question of ‘What is a woman?’"

Reid reemphasized how this should not be addressed from a "WNBA values" perspective, like how the task force is said to be tackling this, but "If we address it from a medical evidence perspective… We don’t have to have these huge task forces. We just know medical transitions do not work."

Reid finished her thought with, "This is not a liberal or a right issue. This is also not a gay or straight issue. I’m a lesbian, my entire coalition is gay and lesbians… Most Americans know that [transitioning] kids is not right. This is a common sense American issue where Sophie Cunningham just said what we already knew in the Midwest."

Social media influencer Becky Weiss, who has 1.2 million followers on Instagram, told me: "I've been speaking out against the extreme LGBTQ ideology, especially targeted at children."

Weiss also had high praise for Cunningham. "I love what Sophie is doing, taking a stand for little girls, grown women in women’s sports, because they deserve to play on a fair playing field. Boys simply do not belong. It’s not controversial. It’s just literally common sense."

When discussing what she’d tell the commissioner, Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams, Minnesota Lynx Head Coach Cheryl Reeve, Weiss said, "There’s no such thing as a trans child. A kid only thinks they’re trans if someone grooms them, groomed them, or indoctrinated them to believe they are trans… Men don’t belong in women’s bathrooms, in women’s sports, in women’s locker rooms. And kids certainly don’t need to have any of this in their lives."

This group, which seems to grow every game they rally, is a great example on how to agree to disagree. They find common ground on a vital issue that is affecting women and girls, and yes, boys too as Jamie Reid and her team emphasized in our conversations.

Kara Dansky even believes in aspects of White privilege. I think it’s nonsense. But we shook hands and are happy to link arms in the fight to protect women’s sports and spaces. That’s how America should be.

Let’s hope as rally organizer Amy Sousa told me that she hopes the "pressure that we put on them (WNBA), will make them stand up and do the right thing." You don’t need weeks or months, WNBA. The league is for females only. Just state the common sense that the vast majority of America affirms.

In the meantime, these women, and a few men, will continue to organize across the country, showcasing a lost art of linking arms on an important issue, while not allowing petty politics to ruin the progress they’ve made.

item.title: Former Disney star David Henrie rejected 'secular' Hollywood lifestyle after life-changing monastery visit
item.description: David Henrie reveals how Kevin James invited him to a monastery in 2012, leading to a general confession that transformed his faith and worldview.
item.content:encoded:
Former Disney star David Henrie is opening up about how he rejected the "secular" Hollywood lifestyle after going on a life-changing monastery visit.

Earlier this week, the "Wizards of Waverly Place" star was a guest on Raymond Arroyo's "Arroyo Grande" podcast and discussed how his friendship with fellow actor Kevin James led to him discovering his faith.

"I started changing my whole perspective on life and faith. I so craved an objective belief system. I grew up in relativistic Hollywood and, you know, a partying lifestyle, secular life, worldliness, materialism, and it left me empty," Henrie said.

"I call it the bubblegum theory of pleasure. Every time you eat a piece of bubblegum, it loses its flavor. In a few moments, you pop another one in. At the end of the day, you've gone through the whole pack, and now you just feel worse than you did when you started. That was me before I met Kevin," he continued.

HEATHER LOCKLEAR SAYS SHE LIVES 'FAR AWAY' FROM HOLLYWOOD AND STAYS OUT OF THE SOCIAL SCENE

Henrie detailed that he found God during this time, and James extended an invitation to him to visit St. Michael's Abbey in Orange County in 2012 and do his general confession.

"And I was like, 'What's that?' So, I learned about what it was, and I wrote a whole chapter book to bring to the priest there," Henrie said.

Henrie told Arroyo that he felt "so relieved" after his monastery visit with James.

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: Karoline Leavitt’s lasting legacy is opening the White House to indie press
item.description: Karoline Leavitt's legacy as White House press secretary centers on opening the briefing room to new media voices and independent content creators.
item.content:encoded:
At the end of the month, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will end a tenure that many consider to be one of the best in the 97-year history of the office. Importantly, she will leave something behind — a vital legacy of opening the briefing room to independent media.

Leavitt handled her office with grace and dexterity, no mean feat for someone communicating for President Donald Trump, who talks more than a morning radio disc jockey. Somehow, she was never in front of his messaging, but also never far behind.

As a queen of cool, Leavitt could not be flustered. She always had an air of confidence and, dare I say, levity. Even when her occasional jocular barbs were tossed at reporters, they rarely turned into acrimony.

SCRAMBLE FOR KAROLINE LEAVITT'S REPLACEMENT ENSUES WITH JUST WEEKS UNTIL TRUMP'S SPOKESPERSON EXITS

Beyond serving as a model for future press secretaries, Leavitt’s strongest legacy will be her commitment to opening up the White House media ecosystem to small indie news outlets and even social media influencers.

Every press conference opens with a question from the "new media seat," a practice that was much maligned early on by fussy old legacy outlet reporters who rolled their eyes at these commoners gaining entry to their fancy club.

I recall a friend of mine, who was new to the briefing room, telling me of an old regular huffing and puffing and saying, "This is where I stand, you have to move!"

She did not move.

WHITE HOUSE PUSHED FOR PROTOCOL TO PRESERVE CORRESPONDENTS' CREDIBILITY AFTER TRUMP'S SECRET PLANE SWITCH

How gauche it was, having mere bloggers or TikTok personalities with this kind of access to the most powerful office in the world. But Leavitt understood that in today’s media, those voices now have as much purchase as major newspapers once did.

It was bumpy at times; the early rollout of binders with files of information on Jeffrey Epstein turned out to be more walk of shame than victory lap. But much more often, these newer outlets were bringing questions to the fore that the legacy media tend to ignore — not through negligence, but because they aren’t niche outlets.

Leavitt understands that the White House press briefing room is a two-way street. Its main function may be to get the president’s message to the people, but the press also brings the concerns of the people to the White House in the form of questions. Influencers, though merrily mocked, have a very direct relationship with their audiences.

Especially younger audiences.

I asked Andrew Kolvet, spokesperson for Turning Point USA — which has a firm focus on educating young voters — about Leavitt’s tenure, and he told me, "She has forced legacy news media to work harder to keep up while opening up multiple seats to new media voices who have had to raise their fact-checking and editorial games in a space that desperately needs it. She sparred with them all in viral exchanges that became must-watch news, even for college kids scrolling their phones."

Kolvet also couldn’t quite resist adding, "As a TPUSA alumni, she was a happy warrior just like Charlie [Kirk]."

Leavitt brought in voices such as Andy Ngo, who has been warning of the advance of Antifa activists for years, and we have seen more of these violent thugs put away — including a leader in Texas who received 100 years in prison for attacking an ICE facility.

Meanwhile, activist reporters like Nick Shirley have been given much attention from Leavitt’s comms shop. He and those like him have revealed potentially billions of dollars in fraud.

WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS WIDELY PRAISE KAROLINE LEAVITT AS SHE ANNOUNCES EXIT FROM TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

The reason that opening the White House press briefing room to independent news media and content creators is Leavitt’s greatest achievement is that, in all likelihood, it will survive not just her moving on, but long after the Trump administration is gone — no matter which party takes power.

This is because, even if a Democrat wins, it will be a tough sell to start kicking out these outlets that the country has been accustomed to hearing from. Even for the left, such a move would probably be too censorious to try.

Yes, Leavitt is a gifted communicator who can be spoken of in the same breath as great press secretaries such as Tony Snow and Ari Fleischer. But ultimately, her greatest contribution is opening the door for new media, and by extension, those this new media represents.

Leavitt will be missed, but her dedication to giving every voice in the media a fair shot at the White House will stay with us for a long time to come.

item.title: Lions betting outlook for 2025: why the NFC North division title is the best play at +170
item.description: Jahmyr Gibbs and Amon-Ra St. Brown lead the Lions as they aim to reclaim the NFC North division after a frustrating 4-6 second-half collapse.
item.content:encoded:
Last season, it was fairly easy to make an argument that the best division in the NFL was the NFC North. All of the teams in that division were able to win nine games, but the Vikings and the Lions missed the postseason. Will the Lions find a way back into the playoffs this year, or will it be another down year?

I was pretty high on the Lions going into the season last year. I didn’t expect them to take a step back, and for the first portion of the season, I think I was correct. They lost Ben Johnson to the Bears, but I still thought the team would be good with all of their weapons and their defense. The Packers beat them to start the season, and their only other loss in the first seven weeks was to the Chiefs. After the bye week, the wheels kind of fell off as they went 4-6 over their final 10 games. Only one of the final six losses was by more than one score, so perhaps there can be some positive regression coming their way this year.

DETROIT LIONS GREAT FRANK RAGNOW DETAILS HIS ABRUPT RETIREMENT, FAILED COMEBACK ATTEMPT

As mentioned, with Johnson taking over the Bears, the Lions didn’t have quite as crisp an offense, but they did add Drew Petzing this season, and that should help the offense take a step forward. The team had some changes on the offensive line, but they also did put some moves in place to address it. One change that should be interesting is that they sent away David Montgomery to the Texans. They replaced him with Isiah Pacheco, who is not quite the bruiser that Montgomery was. Aside from that, they gave an extension to a couple of guys, but nothing major.

I have to imagine that the team, looking at last year’s performance and those close games, thinks they can just make small adjustments in order to get back to the postseason. Without Montgomery, the ball should be in their star, Jahmyr Gibbs’ hands even more. Amon-Ra St. Brown is one of the best wide receivers in the league, and Jared Goff has hooked up with him repeatedly. With a strong offensive line, the Lions offense could be very dynamic. On defense, it probably comes down to health. Aidan Hutchinson is a great defensive end, and they have some solid linebackers. I do have concerns about the secondary, but overall they should be fine.

They have a win total of 10.5, and their schedule sets up fairly well to get those wins. I’m not sure I want to get too involved with it though. I probably would prefer to play them to win the division at +170. I think their schedule is easier than the Bears and Packers, which might mean they only need to beat out the Vikings, a team with a quarterback battle. Another interesting one is for them to have three wins after five games at +170. They faced the Saints, Bills, Jets, Panthers, and Cardinals. The Saints and Jets are at home, and I think both will be wins. I don’t know that they will beat the Bills and Panthers on the road, but they should beat Arizona. item.title: Carmen Electra reveals what she wants in a man after racy Playboy comeback
item.description: "Baywatch" star Carmen Electra opens up about dating, confidence and what she truly wants in a partner after her stunning Playboy comeback three decades later.
item.content:encoded:
After making her Playboy comeback, Carmen Electra says she’s open to hopping back into the dating pool.

At 54, the "Baywatch" bombshell posed for the magazine three decades after her debut. The actress and model first appeared in the magazine in 1996 at age 24 and now graces the pages of its Summer 2026 issue, which is on sale now.

Posing in fishnets, Electra also answered readers' burning questions about love — but she isn't just dishing out dating advice. She's ready for a romance of her own.

MARTHA STEWART GETS CANDID ABOUT PLASTIC SURGERY, DATING AS SHE TURNS 85

"I still like a guy that's a little bit edgy, but I wouldn't mind being with a dad type," the star told Fox News Digital. "I did actually date a dad. He had a daughter. I fell in love with the daughter. And I kind of thought that was going to be the relationship. Didn't work out, but I could be with someone who has a kid or not."

The actress and model has walked down the aisle twice before. She wed former NBA star Dennis Rodman in November 1998. Rodman filed for an annulment just nine days later, though the pair reconciled before Electra ultimately filed for divorce in April 1999.

Electra gave marriage another shot with Jane's Addiction guitarist Dave Navarro, saying "I do" in 2003. The couple announced their separation in 2006, and their divorce was finalized in 2007.

CARMEN ELECTRA REVEALS HER SIMPLE RULE FOR KEEPING THE ‘SPARK ALIVE’ IN RELATIONSHIPS

Today, Electra isn't putting any limits on love.

"They don't have to be a dad," she said. "They could be a little bit younger. I don't know. I don't really know who that guy is yet. I work really hard. I make money. I'm not looking for the man with money. That's not my goal. If he wants to buy me a few gifts, that's nice. But I can take care of myself. He just has to be a good person. That's very important. And we have to like the same things."

"It's also cool when opposites attract," she noted. "Because they say if two people are too similar, one person is unnecessary. So you don't want it to be too similar, but you do want to like certain things. You want to have some things in common. But you also want to learn from each other."

Electra has long worn her heart on her sleeve — and "love" on her skin. The pinup previously told Fox News Digital she has the word tattooed on her wrist.

"I've always been about love," Electra said at the time. "I've always come from a place of love. And if we could all do that, what a wonderful place we could be in. If you really mess with me, I don't know how much love you're going to get. But I truly believe in love."

Electra said she has felt plenty of love from her social media followers, who have cheered her on through the years.

"Look, sometimes I'm trying different things on my Instagram page," she said. "Not everyone's going to love those things, and you might not get as many likes. But you turn around and boom, my fans are there."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

After making a splash in Hollywood, Electra has discovered what makes her feel most confident, and it has nothing to do with looking glamorous or having a beau. For her, it's all about being booked and busy.

"I feel the most confident when I'm working, and I've been working a lot," she said. "When I'm working, I'm really happy. It's weird; you would think that by now I'd be over it. But I'm just not. I love it. And the more I work, the more confident I feel. When I'm in love, I feel confident. But I don't have someone in my life right now. But I'm still confident because I'm working."

After returning to Playboy, Electra has a message for women who think getting older means fading into the background: Don't buy it.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Don't let anyone tell you you're too old," she said. "That's a myth. You are living your own life. You're not living your life for other people. And honestly, if you're manifesting that, that's what it's going to be for you. You have to change your thought process. You have to start telling yourself every morning, 'I'm beautiful. I'm good enough. I look great. I'm pretty.' Whatever it is that you want to be, you can be that."

"At one time in my life, I was reading a lot of books about Buddhism," she reflected. "I remember one book talked about your inner child and never losing your inner child. item.title: Archaeologists uncover mysterious face hidden for centuries in Book of Revelation city
item.description: A 7.2-foot marble statue from the Book of Revelation city of Sardis was found face-down by excavators — its rare Lydian features preserved for 2,500 years.
item.content:encoded:
A rare, 2,500-year-old marble statue has emerged from the ruins of Sardis, an ancient city immortalized in the Book of Revelation.

The discovery, which dates to the fifth century B.C., was announced by the Turkish Ministry of Culture and Tourism earlier in August. Sardis is located in the Salihli district of Manisa, about 45 miles east of the major Turkish city of İzmir.

Pictures show excavators carefully uncovering the monumental statue, which still retained well-preserved facial features, at the archaeological site.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNEARTH SECRET CHURCH TIED TO COUNCIL OF NICAEA, CHRISTIANITY'S DEFINING MOMENT

The statue depicts a young man and measures around 7.2 feet tall.

In a translated social media post, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy described the find as an "extraordinary discovery."

He noted that the statue was repurposed as paving along a colonnaded street during the Roman period and was positioned face-down, helping protect its features for centuries.

"The unusual details of its clothing bear traces of Lydian culture," said Ersoy.

AUTHOR DINESH D'SOUZA CHALLENGES BIBLE SKEPTICS WITH 'STARTLING' ARCHAEOLOGICAL DISCOVERIES

"The statue, which appears to be holding a fruit in its hand, provides important evidence that will contribute to our understanding of life, religious beliefs and cultural interactions in Sardis during the period."

In a translated statement, officials described the statue as having "larger-than-life dimensions [that] make it a rare example from the period."

"The young man is depicted wearing a thick himation, a thin chiton, and beneath them a distinctive garment featuring horizontal lines," the translated statement said.

"This type of clothing is not seen on comparable statues from Anatolia and Greece, highlighting the work’s local characteristics and its connection to Lydian culture."

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNEARTH ANCIENT TREASURE CACHE AT BIBLICAL CITY CONNECTED TO GENESIS

Sardis was once the capital of the ancient Lydian Kingdom before later becoming an important center of the Persian Empire, the period to which the statue dates.

The city is named as one of the seven churches in Asia Minor addressed by Jesus Christ in the Book of Revelation.

Revelation 3:1–6 begins, "To the angel of the church in Sardis write..."

The other churches included Ephesus, Pergamum, Thyatira, Smyrna, Philadelphia and Laodicea.

Ancient marble statues were often painted, and researchers plan to examine the Sardis statue for any surviving traces of pigment.

The artifact is covered in a thick layer of hardened deposits, which conservators will remove with care while protecting any remaining paint.

Specialists will also examine the surrounding soil for traces of color.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Once conservation and restoration are complete, the statue will be displayed at the Manisa Museum in western Turkey.

The discovery is the latest in a series of archaeological finds from ancient cities mentioned in the Book of Revelation.

Earlier this summer, an ancient mosaic was uncovered in Smyrna, an archaeological site in modern-day İzmir, Turkey.

In Ephesus, archaeologists found a Roman-era marble bathtub and a fragment of a male statue that had been reused as a paving stone.

item.title: Jeff Arcuri reveals how 'Bachelorette' wife’s cancer fight transformed his comedy — and their marriage
item.description: Jeff Arcuri's Netflix special tackles his wife Katie Thurston's stage IV breast cancer diagnosis with the same honesty that fueled his crowd work rise.
item.content:encoded:
Life can be uncomfortable. Jeff Arcuri has built a career on finding the joke in uncomfortable moments.

"I think you can make anything funny. You can make awkwardness funny if you’re just honest. People respond to the honesty," the comic told Fox News Digital.

That philosophy has been shaped by nearly two decades of stand-up, but the last few years have tested it in ways Arcuri could not have scripted. As his career surged toward his first special, "Jeff Arcuri: Nice to Meet You," now streaming on Netflix, his personal life grew more complicated when his wife, "Bachelorette" alumna Katie Thurston, was diagnosed with stage IV breast cancer.

"The past two years with my wife kind of grew me up a little bit," Arcuri said. "So my comedy kind of matured, and that’s what the special is. The first half is the stuff that I found funny, and the second half is a lot of s--- that really happened to me."

LAWYER-TURNED-SOCIAL MEDIA SENSATION IS BETTING IT ALL ON GOD, LOVE AND GRIEF

Rather than rely on material he had accumulated over years, Arcuri said he wanted the special to reflect the reality he was actually living.

"There’s no way I’m going to do a special not talking about what’s going on in my current life right now."

Long before Arcuri applied that philosophy to deeply personal material, it was central to the crowd work that helped him gain a following online.

He said he often prefers engaging with someone who appears reluctant to participate rather than the person eager to become part of the show.

"I want him, because now if he laughs, I win," Arcuri said. "He’s going to answer honestly, thinking it’s going to throw me off. But in reality, he’s probably going to only build it, because a truthful audience member is the most valuable, hilarious thing."

That belief in honesty created a challenge in "Nice to Meet You": telling jokes that were true to his experience without bumming out the crowd. He needed to make it safe for viewers to laugh when the subject matter became serious.

Arcuri recalled saying during the special that one of the hardest parts of his wife’s illness was getting her to laugh, "because that’s all I got."

The line was not necessarily intended as a joke, he said, and audiences at most of the tapings did not treat it like one. But one crowd laughed.

"I guess I’m that good," he jested, noting that small adjustments in delivery can make huge changes in the show. It didn't mean pretending the underlying experience was not serious.

COMEDIAN DES BISHOP ON HOW AMERICA MADE HIM FUNNIER AND HIS 'HEALTHY COLLABORATION' WITH WIFE HANNAH BERNER

That approach extended beyond the stage. Asked whether he was comfortable discussing his wife’s diagnosis, Arcuri responded plainly, "Yeah. I put it on Netflix."

He said he and Thurston have found value in talking openly about what they are experiencing rather than treating cancer as a forbidden subject. Thurston shares cancer updates on her Instagram account, which Arcuri said is followed by a lot of women going through their own experiences with illness. She tends to be very transparent about her diagnosis and treatment — perhaps too transparent.

Arcuri said he sometimes learns updates about his wife through her Instagram broadcast page. "Call me first!" he joked.

Poking fun at the situation is key to the couple's coping strategy. He recounted one of his wife's quips that made his father spit his food out.

"My wife gave me Lactaid at the dinner table because I forgot it in my hotel room ... I go 'Oh, thank you, my angel.' And she said, 'Don't call me that, I ain't dead yet!'"

Arcuri resisted describing that material as "dark comedy," since he didn't write it with that in mind. Rather, he simply wanted his act to be true to his life.

"If anything, I had to make light of something hard," he said.

WITH 10 KIDS AT HOME, COMEDIAN KOUNTRY WAYNE SAYS REAL LIFE WRITES THE JOKES

Arcuri’s current ease onstage came after years in which success was far less certain.

The comic got his start in comedy around 2009 or 2010, he said, after which he spent some time telling jokes in Michigan before moving to Chicago for more stage time and then to the Big Apple, where he got the opportunity to appear on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert."

"I did a s---ty job at that. I did a bad job."

What followed was what he described as "the most depressive comedy years of my entire life."

"I thought I was going to make it when I came here, and I just ate it for two years straight."

But booking shows on cruise ships and developing relationships with other New York comedians culminated in an audition for the famous Comedy Cellar, and performing there gave him the confidence to start posting his work online.

The past two years also forced Arcuri to recognize that humor could not carry every emotional burden.

While his career took him around the world, Thurston was navigating cancer treatment. Arcuri said therapy helped him manage what it meant to support someone through that experience while handling his own fear.

"I was her person and she was my person, but also there’s a lot you go through being adjacent to somebody that’s going through that," he said.

He found himself repeatedly reassuring his wife that things would be all right.

"I’m telling her that, ‘We’re going to be OK,’" he said. "But I’m telling her that — who’s telling me that?"

Eventually, he told Thurston something he had struggled to admit.

"I’m afraid about your health and it freaks me out. And sometimes I pretend to be stronger than I am."

Arcuri said he had worried that showing that fear would change how his wife saw him.

"I was so scared she wouldn’t see me as a man if I wasn’t like, ‘It’s going to be okay.’"

Instead, she thanked him for saying it.

For a comedian whose instinct is almost always to seize the funny moment, it was another kind of honesty.

For all the ways Arcuri says his comedy has matured, his instinct to find the joke has not gone anywhere. And Thurston helps him turn real life into new material.

He called her "my muse and my biggest inspiration and my biggest motivator with comedy."

Arcuri recalled walking out of the bathroom in a revealing robe when Thurston reacted by calling him "Flabio" instead of "Fabio."

"Your subconscious roasted me. You said 'Flab-io' and you didn't realize," Arcuri recalled saying to his wife.

"She was mortified. And then the next thing she said was, 'Write that down.'"

Even the title of his debut special was inspired by a real habit he hadn't planned. His manager pointed out that the comedian routinely said, "Nice to meet you," to people he called on in the crowd during his shows.

"I watched through it, and it’s like, ‘Hey, nice to meet you. I’m Jeff,’" over and over, he recalled.

"It’s also my debut special," he added. "So it’s those two things mixed in."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

After years of trying jokes, bombing, rebuilding and finally finding an audience, the title doubles as a fitting introduction to the next phase of his career.

And if Arcuri’s philosophy holds, whatever comes next — awkward, difficult or otherwise — will probably end up in the act.

item.title: New York Magazine severs ties with writer Ross Barkan, updates 67 columns following plagiarism probe
item.description: New York Magazine announced it has severed ties with columnist Ross Barkan after plagiarism accusations surfaced, leading updates to 67 of his pieces.
item.content:encoded:
New York Magazine announced Friday it has severed ties with columnist Ross Barkan after launching an investigation into plagiarism allegations.

"After an independent editorial review, New York found that Ross Barkan did not adhere to our editorial standards, and we have updated 67 columns that did not include proper attribution of language, information, and/or sourcing," the publication said in a statement obtained by Semafor. "We have updated our archives to include proper attribution in all of the stories that our review found previously inadequate, noting that those updates were made, and are committed to addressing any other instances that come to light."

"Upon conclusion of the review, we have determined that we will no longer publish his column. We regret that this work did not live up to our editorial standards, and apologize to the writers whose work was not properly attributed," the magazine added.

NEW YORK MAGAZINE COLUMNIST ACCUSED OF PLAGIARISM BY FELLOW REPORTERS, TRIGGERS INTERNAL REVIEW

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Barkan wrote, "We've decided to end the column and I send all the best to New York Magazine. In the course of nearly 250 pieces, there were times I should have been more careful with citation. I'm sorry about these errors and will work to do better, more careful in the future."

Barkan also teased a new column he plans to launch in September.

Vox Media, New York Magazine's parent company, did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

OLIVIA NUZZI EXITS NY MAGAZINE FOLLOWING RFK JR. RELATIONSHIP REVELATIONS

The controversy began in May when Washington Post reporter Drew Harwell accused Barkan of lifting from his report about conservative commentator Ben Shapiro and his outlet The Daily Wire for one of his columns.

After Harwell highlighted the similarities between the two articles, New York Magazine updated its piece with an editor's note offering credit to the Washington Post, though Harwell explained he wasn't "entirely sure what happened."

COLLEGE STUDENT AT THE CENTER OF NY MAGAZINE HIT PIECE ON YOUNG CONSERVATIVES SPEAKS OUT

NPR correspondent Bobby Allyn found additional examples of what appeared to be Barkan lifting similar phrases and descriptions from The Intercept and Compact Magazine on other reports.

"The paragraphs in question are summarizing the historical background or context of the stories, with some instances containing the same 30 words in a row, or near identical passages with a word or phrase slightly tweaked," Allyn wrote.

Barkan was initially defiant in response to critics, telling Fox News Digital at the time he "did not plagiarize anyone" and "[a]ll of this is ridiculous."

Fox News' Lindsay Kornick contributed to this report.

item.title: Carly Simon seemingly takes aim at ex James Taylor on new album as she sings 'Maybe I never loved you'
item.description: Carly Simon's new album "Comes in Waves" features a track that appears aimed at ex-husband James Taylor, questioning whether their love ever existed.
item.content:encoded:
Carly Simon appears to take aim at her ex-husband James Taylor with a five-word bombshell: "Maybe I never loved you."

The Grammy-winning singer seems to turn the wreckage of their decade-long marriage into a song on her new album, "Comes in Waves."

"Maybe I never loved you / But anyway, I thought I did," Simon sings on the album’s second track. "I married you, we had a kid / That counts for something."

‘YOU’RE SO VAIN’ SINGER CARLY SIMON SAYS PARKINSON’S AND CANCER DIAGNOSES KEPT HER FROM PUBLIC EYE

She immediately undercuts her own certainty, wondering whether she did love her former husband — and whether he ever truly loved her.

"Maybe I never loved you / Yes, and maybe I did," she sings. "And maybe you never loved me / Although God knows, you said you did."

Taylor is never identified by name.

Simon was married to the "Fire and Rain" singer from 1972 to 1983. Their relationship was rocky and remained in the public eye for decades.

"You came for me those times I hid / I’m so glad you did that," she sings. "And maybe it’s wrong to wonder how everything kind became forbidden."

The song eventually concludes with what sounds like a final attempt at closure.

"And maybe it’s best to bury whatever it was we had our fill of," she sings. "Maybe I never loved you / Maybe I always will."

Fox News Digital has reached out to both Simon and Taylor for comment.

In a 2015 interview with People, Simon said she and Taylor had not spoken in more than a decade.

"I still want to heal him, I still want to make him all right," she said. "And I love him so much."

Simon said Taylor's treatment of her had been deeply painful, but writing her memoir helped her understand something about herself and about unrequited love.

IN MEMOIR, CARLY SIMON REVEALS SHE USED 'SPANISH WITCH DOCTOR' TO HELP SAVE HER MARRIAGE

"My incredible loyalty to him, in spite of the fact that he has treated me without any regard, has been so painful to me for so long," she told the outlet. "But, through the course of writing the book, I really started to understand that I could love and not be loved. And that was the big realization for me, that it doesn’t have to be a two-way street."

The deeply personal album arrives as Simon has also been navigating significant health challenges away from the spotlight.

The "You’re So Vain" singer has Parkinson’s disease and recently had surgery for basal cell carcinoma, a form of skin cancer.

Simon explained to People why she had largely stayed out of the public eye.

"It has taken me some time to understand the diagnosis, to adjust to it, and to decide how much I wanted to say about it publicly," the 83-year-old told the outlet in a statement published July 27.

"Parkinson's is different for everyone, and it can be unpredictable," she continued. "Some days I'm so tired I can't get the day moving at all. On others, it gives me a little more room to move, think, work and feel like myself."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Her comments offer a rare glimpse into what the legendary singer has been experiencing privately while continuing to create music.

Her latest project, "Comes in Waves," marks the end of an 18-year hiatus from releasing original music — and she's looking squarely at the past while confronting the realities of the present.

Simon and Taylor were one of music's ultimate power couples of the 1970s.

Their romance moved fast. Simon said she went to Taylor's dressing room at New York's Carnegie Hall in 1971 after seeing him perform.

"I have a wonderful history with Carnegie Hall," she said previously in a Harper’s Bazaar interview. "I met James there that same year when I went to his dressing room to say hello, and he invited himself to my home for a late-night lunch that expanded into a life together."

By the following year, they were married.

Their wedding took place on Nov. 3, 1972, in a small ceremony at Simon's New York home.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

But the marriage didn't last.

The couple separated in 1981, and their divorce was finalized in 1983. They share two children, Sally Taylor and Ben Taylor.

Behind the scenes, their marriage was unraveling as Taylor struggled with drug addiction. Both Simon and Taylor have acknowledged infidelity during their marriage.

Simon later described their relationship in her 2015 memoir, "Boys in the Trees," as "far from the idyllic one that the general public reads about."

She had an even harsher description of their relationship.

"Our love became bipolar, switching from love to hate, lust to loathing, and back again, sometimes within a day," Simon wrote.

Taylor has also acknowledged how deeply his addiction damaged his relationships.

"You could fall in love, but if one of the people is addicted, it’s not going to work," he told Parade. "The whole person is simply not available."

item.title: Chiefs heiress Gracie Hunt reveals why she lifts heavy weights — and doesn’t count calories
item.description: Gracie Hunt reveals her farmer's litmus test for clean eating and explains why heavy strength training replaced marathon running in her fitness routine.
item.content:encoded:
Kansas City Chiefs heiress Gracie Hunt recently opened up about her health philosophy on "The Riley Gaines Show," revealing that heavy strength training and a simple approach to nutrition keep her energized and confident.

Speaking on a recent episode of the podcast, the former Miss Kansas USA and marathon runner dispelled misconceptions around women's fitness — specifically the belief that lifting heavy weights leads to a bulky physique.

"There's so much misconception out there that if you lift weights, you're going to be bulky and big," Hunt told host and women's sports advocate Riley Gaines. "That is not how it works."

KAI TRUMP REVEALS DIET AND NUTRITION SECRETS THAT CREATED SIX-PACK ABS POST-SURGERY

Hunt said that over the past three years, her routine has changed significantly, as she stepped back from long-distance running to focus more on heavy strength training.

"When you have enough muscle, you can sustain a healthy diet with lots of variety," the former pageant queen noted, adding that building muscle eliminates the need to track every calorie or macronutrient.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Instead of relying on meal tracking, Hunt said she applies a sort of litmus test to determine whether a food fits into her clean-eating lifestyle.

"If I was a farmer, could I grow this or make this?" she asks herself. "If I don't know how to make it, maybe I shouldn't eat it."

Hunt's passion for physical fitness began early in life, she told Gaines. Originally, she planned to go into competitive soccer, but her athletic trajectory changed after she suffered multiple concussions. The injuries forced her to pivot away from soccer into pageantry, marathons and strength training.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Reflecting on her shift away from competitive team sports, the football heiress emphasized how physical activity shaped her self-image and mental resilience.

"Sports empower women," Hunt said. "They teach you how to be healthy and also to not attach health and wellness to how you look and to vanity. It's more about, 'Am I healthy? How can I perform?'"

She said she believes that physical strength fosters body confidence, regardless of societal standards.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"I'm strong. So even if I don't look like what society idolizes as beauty, I'm confident in my skin because I know I'm strong."

For women seeking a healthy, strength-focused routine, Hunt recommends building workouts around consistent weightlifting, balanced with high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and a favorite form of cardio, whether that's hiking, walking or trail running.

Above all, physical fitness should be viewed as a long-term lifestyle aimed at overall well-being, not just a quick goal to hit, according to Hunt.

"Fitness isn't about reaching a certain aesthetic and calling it a day — it's about pursuing a life where you can be your best for everyone else around you," she said. "Find something that you love and can do for life."

item.title: Spain stocks African enclave Ceuta with boosted security as Morocco monitors calls for second border rush
item.description: Spain's African enclave Ceuta sees soldiers patrolling streets as Morocco says it arrested those inciting a second mass border crossing on Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
Spain and Morocco have beefed up security on both sides of the border in Spain's African enclave Ceuta as renewed calls circulate social media for Moroccan migrants to rush the border a second time after an initial mass migration event in July overwhelmed the city.

Soldiers patrolled the city's commercial and government buildings Friday while an enhanced police presence could be seen on Ceuta's main avenues, Reuters reported.

On the Moroccan side, security personnel dressed in all-black patrolled the beaches of Fnideq, one of the most prominent launching points from which migrants illegally entered Ceuta on July 30 as part of a mass migration event that saw over 70,000 people rush into Ceuta from Morocco.

The strengthened security followed calls on social media for Moroccans to again rush into Ceuta, and into Spain's other African enclave, Melilia, on Saturday.

FIREBRAND REP UNLOADS ON SOCIALIST PRIME MINISTER AS 'HORDES OF MILITARY AGED MEN' SWARM EUROPEAN COUNTRY

"The Ministry of the Interior has detected, during the last few days, the circulation of anonymous publications and messages on certain social networks inciting the organization of attempts at collective and illegal crossing to the cities of Ceuta and Melilla, practices which carry serious risks to the safety of people and aim to instrumentalize migration issues in acts of incitement, which are criminalized by law," Morocco's Ministry of the Interior said in a statement posted to the country's state-affiliated news website MAP.

Morocco arrested multiple people who circulated the inciting statements, Interior Ministry spokesperson Rachid El Khalfi said.

The Interior Ministry also called on Spain to continue working to return the remaining Moroccan migrants in Ceuta back to the North African country.

TRUMP PUTS ASYLUM LAWYERS ‘ON NOTICE’ WITH NEW FRONT IN WAR ON FRAUD

Of the more than 72,000 migrants who rushed the border, the vast majority have returned to Morocco, according to statements from Spain and Ceuta's government. About 5,000 remain, Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told reporters Friday.

Spanish officials have been screening the remaining migrants and have processed roughly 500 asylum seekers' cases, rejecting the vast majority of them, Reuters reported.

Spain has also installed floating barriers in the waters where migrants had previously swam across.

At least 96 people died during the mass migration event.

Fox News Digital contacted the governments of Spain, Morocco and Ceuta for further comment.

Reuters contributed to this report.

item.title: 'The End of Oak Street' Review: Anne Hathaway, Ewan McGregor fight dinosaurs in surprisingly fun movie
item.description: Fox News Digital reviews Warner Bros. Pictures' "The End of Oak Street," starring Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor. Produced by JJ Abrams and directed by David Robert Mitchell.
item.content:encoded:
The year of Anne Hathaway is kicked into hyperdrive. Following the release of the legacy sequel "The Devil Wears Prada 2," the indie art house film "Mother Mary" and on the heels of Christopher Nolan's epic "The Odyssey," the Oscar winner now stars in the new movie "The End of Oak Street" (and she still has another movie slated for this fall!). 

She and Ewan McGregor are Denise and Greg Platt, a not-so-happy couple who put on a happy face for their two teenage children, Audrey and Brian (Maisy Stella and Christian Convery) in their idyllic neighborhood on — you guessed it — Oak Street in Summer 1982. 

One night, a mysterious light floods the outside of their home, and they wake up without any power, running water, and are not even picking up any radio stations. It doesn't take long after Denise and Greg leave the house to figure out something isn't right — there are dinosaurs everywhere. 

‘ONE NIGHT ONLY’ REVIEW: MONICA BARBARO AND CALLUM TURNER CHARM IN HIGH-CONCEPT ROM-COM

The entirety of their neighborhood was somehow transported back to a prehistoric era where the end of the street is literally cut off by a giant cliff with jungles taking over people's backyards. The Platts must fight to survive and find a way back home — if there's even a way back home. 

Someone in Hollywood — possibly writer-director David Robert Mitchell — must've pitched, "What if it's 'Jurassic Park' but set in suburbia?" The premise is totally inexplicable, and that's completely OK, as long as the audience can buy into the premise, even one this absurd. Mitchell's strong execution on a pure entertainment level supersedes the need for a logical explanation. 

‘SPIDER-MAN: BRAND NEW DAY’ REVIEW: TOM HOLLAND, ZENDAYA RETURN FOR ACTION-PACKED, EMOTIONAL SEQUEL

Mitchell, best known for his 2014 breakout horror flick "It Follows," knows how to build up suspense and put together fun action sequences. He's aided by cinematographer Mike Gioulakis, editor John Axelrad and Oscar-winning composer Michael Giacchino, who delivers yet another magnificent score. 

It's no surprise that J.J. Abrams, the producer behind "LOST," the "Cloverfield" trilogy and the recent "Star Trek" and "Star Wars" films, also produced this sci-fi action thriller. 

'THE ODYSSEY' REVIEW: CHRISTOPHER NOLAN GOES EPIC WITH HIS MOST AMBITIOUS FILM TO DATE

Hathaway hits her stride here, arguably more so than any of her other role this year, playing the no-nonsense matriarch of the household, while McGregor brings levity as the perhaps Pollyannaish father. But all of them, including Stella and Convery, take turns kicking dinosaur butt. And some of the dinosaurs are quite terrifying! 

'THE INVITE' REVIEW: SETH ROGEN, OLIVIA WILDE HOST ONE HILARIOUS DINNER PARTY YOU WON'T REGRET ATTENDING

"The End of Oak Street" is a fun, crowd-pleasing wild ride that is full of laughs and suspense that feels like a throwback to the kinds of movies that Hollywood used to make. If you're going to squeeze in one more movie with the family before the kids go back to school, consider this one. 

"The End of Oak Street" is rated PG-13 for some strong violent content, bloody images, some strong language and suggestive material. Running time: 1 hour, 39 minutes. In theaters now.

item.title: Stop making a common burger mistake, chef warns: 'One of the worst things you can do'
item.description: Chef Michael Hawk of the Fontainbleau reveals why soaking your burger bun in grease leads to soggy bread and shares his butter-toasting technique for a golden crust.
item.content:encoded:
Soaking your burger bun in the grease and juices leftover from cooking the patty to add extra flavor may seem intuitive, but one chef says it's "one of the worst things you can do."

To form a nice crust on the bun, executive chef Michael Hawk of the Fontainebleau in Miami Beach, Florida, said to toast it in butter to create a barrier that's both flavorful and adds texture.

"Use a sauté pan with medium heat and whole, unsalted butter, melting the butter and putting the bun cut-side down in the pan, applying a little bit of pressure for a little more contact with the pan, and toast it for about two to three minutes, until it's golden brown," Hawk told Fox News Digital.

MEAT EXPERT SHARES THE MISTAKE MOST AMERICANS MAKE WHEN COOKING STEAK

He recommends checking the buns occasionally to make sure they're getting brown enough without burning.

"Ideally, the right time to start toasting your bun is just as your burgers are starting to finish," he said. 

"Burgers, when you pull them off, need a little bit of time to rest so they're not just leeching the liquids out on the bun. If you're going to take the time to make a nice toasty bun, then you don't want to put a liquid right on top of it."

The three or four minutes it takes to get the buns ready is the "perfect amount of time to rest that burger," Hawk said.

Burning burger buns usually happens when people use a grill, according to Hawk, because the heat is much more intense. He advised using a slow, gentle heat to toast the buns. 

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

If using a grill, place them on the outer edges where the surface is less hot.

Hawk's preferred type of bun is brioche or potato bread, because they don't add many additional flavors, allowing for the flavor of the meat to shine through. He said any bun works, though, and people should choose whichever they prefer.

Hawk offered several other dos and don'ts for the perfect burger.

The shape, size and meat blend of a burger are all factors in how to cook it. When cooking a batch of burgers, making them all the same shapes and weights helps, he said.

Hawk advised using a digital thermometer to ensure burgers are cooked precisely and to take them off the heat source 5 degrees before they reach their ideal temperature, since they'll keep cooking while they rest.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Smash burgers continue to be a popular method of cooking burgers, and Hawk said there's only one time people should apply pressure to their patties.

"Smash it as a raw patty," he said. "That's the perfect time to smash it, and the only time you want to smash it."

Once the burger starts to cook, it'll develop a seal on its outer edges that retains the moisture inside, he shared.

"If you smash it halfway through the process, it's going to result in a drier burger, and it's not really going to develop that nice crust, either," Hawk said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Hawk said that pressing the burger while it's cooking is "probably the biggest mistake people make at home."

The other top tip Hawk gave for home cooks is to temper the meat, which not a lot of people do out of concern for bacteria, he acknowledged.

"Allow that burger to come up to room temperature a little bit," he said. 

"Ten to 15 degrees will save you some time on the grill with a much more intense heat source, so it helps you retain more moisture."

item.title: BROADCAST BIAS: Networks turn Trump’s plane switch into a fancy scandal
item.description: The Secret Service advised Trump to switch planes in Turkey, leaving press on Air Force One along with administration officials, sparking days of media outrage.
item.content:encoded:
The coverage of political scandal is one of the most obvious fields of study for anyone looking at media bias. The same people who unconvincingly claimed President Barack Obama's presidency was "largely scandal-free" can manufacture a scandal a day under President Donald Trump.

The allegedly outrageous scandal of this week happened in Turkey, where the Secret Service advised Trump to switch to a different military plane to fly home while the press (and top administration officials) stayed on Air Force One, but were not told the president wasn't on board. As soon as The Washington Post had the story, the anti-Trump spin kicked in. The press were left on a "decoy" plane that could have been shot down by the Iranians.

While the broadcast networks love to open their newscasts with severe weather updates to grab viewer attention, this mini-scandal led CBS and NBC on Tuesday night, and ABC jumped in right after the weather.

WHITE HOUSE PUSHED FOR PROTOCOL TO PRESERVE CORRESPONDENTS' CREDIBILITY AFTER TRUMP'S SECRET PLANE SWITCH

On PBS, "News Hour" anchor Geoff Bennett exemplified the tone: "How unusual is it for the Secret Service to turn Air Force One and its passengers, to include White House staff, the traveling press, into a decoy?" Correspondent Nick Schifrin explained that this happened before with President Bill Clinton in Pakistan in 2000.

On NPR's "Morning Edition" on Wednesday, they brought on former Secret Service agent Robert McDonald, who tried to reassure the audience that he was sure Air Force One still had Air Force protection in the air, so, "I think the premise that those two planes were left out on their own, I think, is a little bit reaching." Anchor Michel Martin resisted: "But you don't know that for a fact." McDonald acknowledged that, but found it hard to believe two Air Force 747s "would be left to fend for themselves."

Journalists went on for days with "decoy" outrage, but it's hard to argue Trump left them in danger, since top aides were still on the plane – Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and domestic policy adviser Stephen Miller, among others.

Everyone in the media knows that covering a president carries the risk of being in the crossfire if someone makes an assassination attempt. They just witnessed it in the first attempt at the White House Correspondents' Dinner this spring.

FETTERMAN SAYS AMERICA MUST TURN DOWN THE TEMPERATURE AFTER WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS DINNER SHOOTING

What's astonishing is how little they seem to care about Trump's vulnerability to assassination, even after he was shot in the ear in one of several foiled attempts to murder him.

On Aug. 4, a 38-year-old California man named Jeanine John Taele was arrested at the Trump National Golf Club Los Angeles after he was spotted taking photos and monitoring security preparations two days before a scheduled visit by the president. Taele had a 16-round magazine with ammunition in his pocket, and authorities recovered a loaded pistol in his car. But in the case of the switched planes, the press sounded like they only worried about their own safety, and they act like Trump endangers himself with his rhetoric and by waging war on terrorist regimes in the Middle East.

Some people thought the Secret Service tactics were grounds for levity. As the story broke on Monday night, MS NOW hosts Rachel Maddow and Lawrence O'Donnell had giggles over the concept of the president being moved from plane to plane on a catering cart, saying that he "lost complete control" of his situation. On Tuesday night, Aug. 11, O'Donnell proclaimed, "No president has ever done more than Donald Trump to reveal himself to be a deeply cowardly man," when he wasn't at all like Harrison Ford's terrorist-punching president in the movie "Air Force One."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Subbing on ABC's "Jimmy Kimmel Live," actor Anthony Anderson wisecracked: "Let's give it up to the Secret Service. Do you know how hard it is to sneak a pig out of Turkey?" He added: "I'm no security expert, but if I was trying to find Donald Trump, a catering truck is the first place I'd look. Next time, hide his ass in a bookmobile."

I was a White House reporter for two years, so I can sympathize with journalists feeling strongly about the concept of being endangered overseas. But they all should understand the Secret Service has a job to do, and it's to keep the president safe. Everyone on that plane was safe. So why did they have to treat it as a scandal? Because manufacturing daily outrages seems to be their job in covering President Trump.
