item.title: ‘I’ll settle for not crazy’: Denver business leaders brace for socialist shift after big win for DSA
item.description: Denver business owners react to the rise of socialist candidates and how their policies could shape the economic landscape in the Colorado capital.
item.content:encoded:
Affordability was a top concern for voters who helped launch democratic socialist candidate Melat Kiros to victory in Denver's Democratic primary in June, defeating 15-term incumbent Diana DeGette. But as democratic socialists gain momentum in Colorado, business owners are grappling with how their progressive policies may collide with the actual costs of running a business in Denver.

"With DSA specifically, I think that too many times, the rhetoric sounds great until it meets the economic realities," J.J. Ament, president and CEO of the Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce, told Fox News Digital. "And by the way, the basic laws of economics, they still apply even at altitude."

Ament runs the oldest and largest chamber of commerce in Colorado, representing the business community. The chamber is nonpartisan and has members from both sides of the political spectrum, he said. 

While the chamber does not endorse individual candidates, Ament noted that it does participate at the member level to promote pragmatic, pro-business candidates, and promote free enterprise and free-market policies.

COLORADO'S SOCIALIST SURGE SHAKES UP THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT

"I tell people sort of as a joke, but not really, that I want pro-business. I'll settle for not crazy," he said.

Colorado, according to Ament, has changed significantly over the past decade or more as the state has come under single-party Democratic control, shifting from one of the top 10 states for business to a place where increasing regulations and higher taxes have made it more difficult to operate a business.

"Those risks could be created whether it's single-party control by Republicans or single-party controlled by Democrats," Ament said. "The reality is where everybody thinks the same, very little thinking actually occurs. And so the trend has been to more regulation, higher fees and taxes, the cost of doing business."

He added that as the city has grown and housing has not kept up, affordability has become a crucial issue, driving up the costs of running a business.

GROCERY BOSS WARNS MAMDANI'S CITY-RUN STORES PIT GOVERNMENT AGAINST 'ITS OWN CITIZENS'

As DSA-backed candidates took seats on the Denver City Council in 2023, the chamber warned that Colorado was becoming "increasingly hostile to business."

Kiros' platform calls for a number of policies affecting the economy, including raising corporate taxes and the federal minimum wage.

Ament believes some DSA-backed policies, like raising the minimum wage, have hurt the very workers and small businesses they were intended to help.

"Just ask any restaurant owner in Denver how the government's interference in minimum wage and tipped wage has helped or hurt the very people, again, it was purported to be designed for," he said. "A lot of times we have policies that are in the name of consumers, but aren't necessarily for consumers."

Ament said the chamber's goal is to help people understand the economic realities of running a business while promoting policies and incentives that make starting a company simpler and less expensive.

JOHN RICH WARNS NASHVILLE'S FAMED BROADWAY COULD GO DARK AS BUSINESSES FACE TAX ‘DEATH NAIL’

"We want every resident here to fully participate in the benefits that come with a thriving economy," he said. "But the choices that are being made are making that even more difficult. We were constantly trying to figure out how to create ladders to crawl over barriers when we just should stop creating the barrier in the first place."

Brad Deen, service manager at Import Mechanics, knows full well the challenges facing small business owners in the area. He said his auto shop has faced increasing problems with crime, drug use, and public safety as the population has boomed.

"It seems like it's directly correlated to the influx of the population to Denver," Deen told Fox News Digital. "Seeing more unhoused and more open-air drug use than I would have in 2004."

Deen was one of several business owners and residents who launched the South Broadway General Improvement District (GID) this year. Community members and businesses voted to impose an additional mill levy tax on themselves to fund private security and cleaning crews in order to make the area more appealing for customers.

MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS

Deen admitted he was reluctant to support additional taxes but felt it was necessary to protect his business.

"As somebody who has kind of railed against tax increases my whole life, this was kind of a different line for me to take, but something that I felt had to be done," he said.

He said the Broadway GID is already making a "huge positive change" by providing 24/7 staff to clean up graffiti and trash. The district has also worked to foster a more collaborative relationship with city leaders, and he noted that police have been more responsive and more present in patrolling the area than in years past.

Deen took a pragmatic approach when considering how DSA policies might affect his business if Kiros wins the election in November.

He said he has benefited and been hurt by policies from both the left and right, and believes no one has all the answers to complex problems like homelessness. If Kiros is elected, he said he would ask her to address encampments outside Denver businesses first.

EXPERT WHO FLED CUBA WARNS OF ‘VICIOUS CYCLE’ THAT WILL LEAD TO ‘COMMUNISTS IN DOUBLE DIGITS’ IN CONGRESS

He expressed some concern about policies supporting higher taxes on corporations eventually being placed upon small businesses and hurting their operations.

"As a relatively large employment group in the city, any large tax increases have a huge impact on us being able to, you know, get staff raises, give bonuses, and provide benefits," Deen told Fox News Digital.

Dealing with crime and rising costs is a challenge also facing Jamie Sanchez, another Denver small-business owner. He runs The Drip Café in Denver's Santa Fe Art District. He also operates a Christian homeless ministry called Recycle God's Love, which he started with his late wife, Carolyn, in 2012.

"I am seeing a lot of businesses turning over and shutting down just through the past three years we've been here," he told Fox News Digital. "So I could imagine why the cost of living here is skyrocketing. I mean, our minimum wage is insane right now to pay baristas to make coffee. So that makes it really difficult. So I can only imagine for some of the other business owners, it's getting really difficult, especially with rent and tax and all that going on. It's definitely been a strain on our business."

Since opening his coffee shop three years ago, Sanchez said he has experienced broken windows, graffiti and threats.

An outspoken Christian, Sanchez drew the ire of a local group called the Denver Communists before his shop even opened, after the group noticed Recycle God's Love called homosexuality a sin in its beliefs section on its website.  

Since then, on every first Friday of the month, protesters from the Denver Communists have held signs and passed out flyers accusing the coffee shop of being run by a "right-wing church" that hates the LGBTQ+ community. Sanchez said "Keep Santa Fe gay" and obscene stickers have also been placed on his windows and doors.

"The Denver Communists specifically have targeted us because of the beliefs that we have," Sanchez told Fox News Digital. "Even though we haven't shown any hate towards these individuals. In fact, we serve people from this group at our homeless outreach. We serve them in our café, we've welcomed them in, we have invited them in, and so our goal is to actually show them the love of God because yeah, we do believe different things, but our approach is to love them in hopes that they would come to Christ."

The Christian shop owner sees the backlash as part of a spiritual battle.

"The reason I come to that conclusion is because a lot of these protesters claim to be Satanists," he told Fox News Digital, adding that he's seen protesters wearing shirts depicting Satan or attacking Jesus. Sanchez said he now holds live worship music in the café every first Friday to help "drown out" the commotion outside.

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

"These groups have decided to twist things and use half-truths to try to stir people in the community to not frequent our coffee shop in hopes that we would not have enough sales to meet rent and that we will shut down," Sanchez said. "And it hasn't been working. In fact, the opposite has been happening to where people are knowing we're here now because of this situation and God has been using it for good."

The Denver Communists told Fox News Digital they were not protesting the café strictly because it is Christian, but because of its religious beliefs about sexuality.

"We are not targeting Christianity, we [are] targeting homophobia and transphobia," a spokesperson for the Denver Communists said. "Sanchez wants to claim Drip’s particular right-wing evangelical fundamentalism is representative of all Christianity, but it’s not. Many Christians are not homophobes and transphobes. Many Christians have joined us in protesting against Drip, including clergy members."

The group, which formed in 2012 as a branch of the International Socialist Organization, told Fox News Digital they view the Drip Café's mission as part of a nationwide, right-wing "coordinated assault ... against the democratic rights and cultural acceptance won by LGBTQ+ people."

"Right-wing churches like Drip Café are key incubators of the homophobia, transphobia, and misogyny that underpin this assault," the group said. "Any effort to make anti-LGBTQ+ bigotry mainstream must be vigorously opposed."

The group is not affiliated with the DSA but shares some broader anti-capitalist and socialist goals promoted by Kiros, such as wealth redistribution and abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Kiros recently brushed aside concerns regarding communists inside the DSA faction of the Democratic Party, telling PBS "Firing Line" host Margaret Hoover there is room in the party for various viewpoints.

"Yeah. Well, some members of the Democratic Party are proudly proclaiming themselves as capitalists, and it’s a big tent, right?" Kiros said. "But, again, at the end of the day, it’s up to the voters, right?"

Kiros denied being a communist, arguing that younger voters are embracing the democratic socialist message because it represents "economic populism."

Jamie Sanchez has concerns about what it could mean for his business if candidates sharing similar viewpoints to those protesting his shop get into local government.

"It definitely is concerning when I hear some of the socialist, communist-type people getting into the local government because of what we've been facing from just national groups who are coming and protesting us," he told Fox News Digital. "So I feel like if they're aligned with that, it is pretty concerning because that would mean that the government eventually would be against this Christian coffee shop essentially. But overall, I trust God and what he's doing, so I don't have any fear about that either."

Melat Kiros's campaign and the Democratic Socialists of America did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: NFL player reveals suspension for Performance Enhancing Drug happened because he was addressing infertility
item.description: Nazeeh Johnson revealed his six-game NFL suspension stems from fertility medications he and his wife used while trying to conceive amid heartbreak.
item.content:encoded:
Nazeeh Johnson's story is a heartbreaker and not because he learned on Friday that the NFL is suspending him six games for violating league policy, but because that violation is apparently linked to the Tennessee Titans player and his wife trying in vain to start their family.

Hours after the NFL announced Johnson would be suspended on Aug. 30 without pay for violating the Performance Enhancing Drug policy, and that he would not be able to return to his team until Oct. 19, Johnson went on social media to explain why he tested positive.

Prepare yourself because this one cuts to the core.

FALCONS' JAMES PEARCE HIT WITH 8-GAME SUSPENSION AS NFL ANNOUNCES WAVE OF BANS ACROSS THE LEAGUE

"My wife and I were trying to conceive a child," Johnson explained on X. "We found out that I was infertile, and I took a fertility medication that was helping me try to conceive a baby.

"I was not aware that there was a substance in the medication that was on the banned list, and I tested positive for a PED."

That isn't the worst part.

A source close to Johnson told Fox News Digital that he and his wife Gabrielle were initially encouraged by the treatments both were taking. It seemed to work. She got pregnant.

But then, tragedy.

"We lost our baby a few weeks ago, and this has been an incredibly difficult time for my wife and me," Johnson said in his post.

Gabrielle shared a post on X showing part of the regimen she underwent to try to get pregnant.

"This is real life," she wrote on a post that includes video of her injecting medication, having eggs harvested, and finally getting a positive pregnancy test result.

"This is a lot of people’s lives," she continued. "It can be a joke or a chance to tear someone down – but for us, it’s our life. There’s no fun in it. Just pain, tears, and recently, disappointment. And that pain doesn’t end when football does."

The suspension is not the first time Johnson's career has suffered a significant setback.

He was drafted by the Kansas City Chiefs in 2022 but was forced to miss all the 2023 season when he tore the ACL in one of his knees during training camp.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

In 2025, the year he and Gabrielle were married, Johnson's season was cut short again when he played only two games due to a shoulder injury.

He signed a one-year contract with the Titans this offseason.

There is, on the surface, no part of this that seems to be anything other than agonizing. But Johnson offered a glimmer of hope in his explanation about the looming suspension.

"Fortunately, we have nine good eggs left," he said. "So we’re holding on to hope that we’ll be able to grow our family."

Johnson also offered some advice to other NFL players before they, too, take any medication for any reason.

"Lesson to all NFL players and new players coming into the league: do not put anything in your body without following the process and getting approval beforehand," he said.

item.title: Virginia State University shooting: At least 5 injured, one critically
item.description: Multiple victims were transported to area hospitals Saturday morning following a shooting near the Quad Annexes at Virginia State University, campus police says.
item.content:encoded:
At least five people were shot at Virginia State University (VSU) on Saturday morning and one remains in critical condition, according to the university and VSU Police.

"Officers responded to the 3300 block of Boisseau Street at approximately 1:28 a.m. and discovered five individuals suffering from gunshot wounds outside VSU residence halls," a university official told Fox News Digital.

"All five were transported to area hospitals. One individual is currently in critical condition. The remaining four sustained non-life-threatening injuries," the official also shared.

VSU police earlier revealed that the shooting occurred near the school's Quad Annexes student housing complex.

STUDENT PERPETRATES DEADLY SHOOTING AT THAILAND HIGH SCHOOL, AUTHORITIES SAY

"A shooting occurred in the area of the Quad Annexes involving multiple victims, who were transported to area hospitals," VSU Police wrote in a statement posted to X.

"Police are on scene and request that you avoid the area," the statement read. 

The university said earlier on X that the shooting involved "multiple suspects." No arrests have been announced.

The campus initially went into lockdown, but the lockdown has now been lifted, according to the university official.

VSU Police said on X that the lockdown was lifted and "normal access to campus may resume."

The shooting occurred on the same day that resident halls opened to returning students on Friday for the school's summer 2026 semester, according to the school's calendar. Classes for the semester will begin on Monday. 

"A significant law enforcement presence remains on campus," a university official told Fox News Digital. 

SEVERAL PEOPLE DEAD, INCLUDING SUSPECT, IN RURAL MICHIGAN MULTI-SCENE SHOOTING: POLICE

Rozia A. Henson Jr., a Democratic member of the Virginia House of Delegates, shared a message on social media praying for the victims and their families.

"Virginia State University is my alma mater. Waking up to this news is heartbreaking. My prayers are with everyone affected this morning, with their families, and with the entire Trojan family. VSU, we are with you," Henson Jr. posted on X.

An investigation into the shooting, led by Chesterfield County Police with assistance from VSU Police, ATF, and the Hanover County Sheriff's Office, is ongoing, a university official told Fox News Digital.

The university is asking anyone with information to contact Chesterfield County Police at 804-748-1251, Crime Solvers at 804-748-0660, or VSU Police at 804-524-5411.

VSU, a state-supported HBCU, is located in Ettrick, Virginia — about 25 miles south of Richmond.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

item.title: Fever coach Stephanie White opens up about fan reception after turbulent week of WNBA controversy
item.description: Stephanie White received a standing ovation Friday after being booed Tuesday, warning that people are trying to tear the Indiana Fever apart.
item.content:encoded:
Indiana Fever head coach Stephanie White ended her week on a high note Friday, after facing immense national scrutiny for days, but still made mention of people trying to "tear" her team apart.

White was cheered by the Indiana crowd ahead of the Fever's game against the Dallas Wings. She had been booed ahead of their most recent game against the New York Liberty on Tuesday, amid controversy over how she initially responded to a flagrant foul on Sophie Cunningham.

But after Cunningham and Caitlin Clark defended White publicly, the fans went back to cheering for the coach on Friday.

FEVER COACH STEPHANIE WHITE DODGES QUESTION ON GOP LETTER ABOUT CAITLIN CLARK’S TREATMENT IN WNBA

"It means a lot, we love eachother in that locker room. And we know that there's a lot of people out there that are trying to tear it apart," White told reporters after the game. "When we say we're a family, we mean that. It doesn't mean we always get along, it doesn't mean we always agree, but at the end of the day it means we circle our wagons and we have each other's back...

"It means a lot to me personally, and obviously, any time you get an ovation from the crowd it's nice too. I think our fans, the true Indiana Fever fans, are amazing. They've been incredible to me for a long time."

White added that the players and coaches on her staff have been "lifting her up."

White's tough week began on last Saturday after her team's game against the Sky in Chicago. When asked about a now-infamous flagrant-2 foul by DiJonai Carrington against Cunningham, White appeared to give Carrington the benefit of the doubt and suggest that the foul wasn't on purpose.

Then ahead of the Fever's Tuesday game against the Liberty, White dedicated her entire pre-game media availability to a rant that sandwiched her admission that she realized the foul was "egregious" in between condemnation of external prognosticators critics.

"For those who have anything to say about the play in the last game, I didn't see the replay. I went straight to a press conference, I thought the play got called right. Thankfully, Sophie is OK. Was it egregious? Absolutely," White said.

"When you get a chance to see that on replay over and over, you see that. I didn't see that in real time. I personally take any suggestions that I don't 100% always have my players back."

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM'S FORMER TEAMMATE APPEARS TO FULLY ENDORSE DIJONAI CARRINGTON'S FLAGRANT FOUL ON FEVER STAR

Clark and Cunningham defended White publicly on Tuesday night.

"Our locker room in there, it's tight, and we have each other's backs," Cunningham said. "Coach loves us...

"She didn't see the clip. At the end of the day, she didn't see the clip."

Clark offered a more personal defense of White.

"I think we forget a lot of times, like, we're human and she has feelings," Clark said. "There's moments that are really hard."

Clark drew from her own experience under intense scrutiny. She told White that even thick skin has limits.

"I've been through the same thing," Clark said. "There's been days where I've been really upset, and you can have the thickest skin in the world, but sometimes it does get to you."

For at least a night, the focus of the Fever's season turned back to basketball on Friday, as Clark and Cunningham led a clean and convincing victory over Paige Bueckers and the Wings.

Indiana has won eight of 10 and finished the night as the league’s fourth-place team, a half-game ahead of the Atlanta Dream — its opponent on Sunday. The Wings have lost seven of 10 to fall into a tie for seventh with Washington.
